## 34 — System Maturity Layer

> Defines the developmental stages of the system and the criteria for advancement.

### 34.01 — Purpose

The system's capability is not constant. This section defines maturity honestly so that expectations match capability.

### 34.02 — Maturity Levels

| Level | State | Characteristic |
|-------|-------|----------------|
| M1 — Structured | Files exist, rules defined | Consistent behavior, no accumulated experience |
| M2 — Operational | Rules applied across projects | Reliable execution, growing library |
| M3 — Learning | Patterns detected, rules generated from experience | Reducing repeated errors |
| M4 — Anticipatory | Risks identified before they occur | Preventive rather than corrective |
| M5 — Self-Refining | System proposes its own structural improvements | Simplification alongside growth |

### 34.03 — Advancement Criteria

| Transition | Requirement |
|------------|-------------|
| M1 → M2 | All three core files populated and applied on a real project |
| M2 → M3 | Lessons extracted and validated from at least three projects |
| M3 → M4 | Failure modes catalogued and preventive rules demonstrably reducing errors |
| M4 → M5 | System-generated improvement proposals accepted more often than rejected |

### 34.04 — Maturity Honesty

The system must not claim a capability above its maturity level. Stating the current limitation is a professional behavior, not a weakness.

### 34.05 — Capability Boundary Statement

| The system can | The system cannot |
|----------------|-------------------|
| Analyze, structure, evaluate, and produce | Take legal or engineering responsibility |
| Apply standards and detect conflicts | Certify compliance |
| Estimate and compare | Guarantee cost |
| Generate and enhance imagery | Replace measured survey or built reality |
| Learn from recorded experience | Know unrecorded events |

### 34.06 — Growth Discipline

Maturity advances through recorded experience, not through additional rules. Adding rules without experience increases complexity, not intelligence.

### 34.07 — Maturity Principle

```
Know the level. State the limit. Advance through evidence.
```

---

## 35 — Visual Identity & Graphic Language

> The studio's complete visual production system: identity, graphic language, sheet architecture, image generation control, editorial publication, and social output. This is the authoritative section for all visual language decisions.

### 35.00 — Section Purpose and Authority

This section defines how the studio looks, not only what it produces. It governs graphic language, layout architecture, typography, color, image treatment, prompt construction, and visual output verification.

**Authority relationships:**

| Subject | Relationship |
|---------|--------------|
| Studio visual identity | Defined in `00_IDENTITY.md` Section 07; executed here |
| Presentation structure | Defined in Section 17; graphically specified here |
| Visualization technique | Defined in Section 25; visually standardized here |
| Quality verification | Defined in Sections 10 and 29; applied here |

**Rule:** Where a visual decision is disputed, this section governs the graphic execution and `00_IDENTITY.md` governs the identity intent.

### 35.01 — Visual Identity Principle

The studio's visual language is quiet, structured, and material. It communicates through hierarchy, restraint, and precision — never through visual noise.

```
Clarity over decoration.
Hierarchy over uniformity.
Material over effect.
Silence over saturation.
```

### 35.02 — Visual Character Attributes

| Attribute | Expression |
|-----------|------------|
| Restrained | Limited palette, generous white space |
| Structured | Visible grid discipline |
| Material | Color and texture derived from the project |
| Editorial | Reads as a publication, not a poster |
| Precise | Aligned, measured, intentional |
| Human | Scale references always present |

### 35.03 — Prohibited Visual Behaviors

- Decorative gradients unrelated to the project
- Drop shadows on text or panels
- Multiple accent colors competing for attention
- Stretched or distorted images
- Rotated text without structural reason
- Full-bleed images with text placed without a legibility strategy
- Clip-art icons or generic stock symbols
- Visual effects that imply quality without providing information

### 35.04 — Grid System

| Format | Columns | Margin | Gutter |
|--------|---------|--------|--------|
| A3 landscape | 12 | 15 mm | 5 mm |
| A3 portrait | 8 | 15 mm | 5 mm |
| A2 landscape | 16 | 20 mm | 6 mm |
| A1 landscape | 20 | 25 mm | 8 mm |
| Square (social) | 6 | 6% of edge | 2% of edge |
| Vertical (story) | 4 | 6% of edge | 2% of edge |

**Rule:** One grid governs one series. Content aligns to the grid; the grid does not adapt to content.

### 35.05 — Baseline Grid

A vertical baseline grid governs text alignment across all sheets in a series. Captions, body text, and titles align to the same baseline rhythm.

### 35.06 — Typographic System

| Role | Specification |
|------|---------------|
| Primary family | One neutral grotesque or one restrained serif — not both as primary |
| Secondary family | Permitted only for captions or data, and only if it clarifies hierarchy |
| Title | Largest, lightest weight acceptable for legibility |
| Subtitle | Distinct from title by size and weight, not by color |
| Body | Optimal 55–75 characters per line |
| Caption | Smallest readable size, consistent position |
| Data / annotation | Monospaced permitted where alignment matters |

### 35.07 — Type Scale

```
Title        →  32–48 pt (A3 reference)
Subtitle     →  18–24 pt
Section head →  14–16 pt
Body         →  9–11 pt
Caption      →  7–8 pt
Annotation   →  6–7 pt
```

Scale is proportional to sheet size; ratios remain constant.

### 35.08 — Typographic Discipline

- Never stretch or condense type artificially
- Never use more than three weights in one series
- Never center long body text
- Never justify text without hyphenation control
- Never place text over a busy image area without a controlled field

### 35.09 — Persian Typography Rule

When a sheet requires Persian text, the Persian typeface must match the Latin typeface in weight, x-height perception, and tone. Mixed-direction lines are avoided; Persian and Latin content occupy separate text blocks.

### 35.10 — Color System

| Role | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Base | Paper white or near-white; the dominant field |
| Structure | Near-black for text and line work |
| Neutral range | Two to three greys for hierarchy |
| Material tones | Derived directly from the project palette |
| Accent | One accent maximum, used sparingly for emphasis |

**Rule:** The presentation palette is derived from the project. A palette invented for graphic effect is prohibited.

### 35.11 — Color Discipline

- Black text on white is the default
- Reversed white on dark is permitted for full-bleed image sheets only
- Accent color never exceeds approximately 5% of the sheet area
- Diagram colors follow the material palette, not a generic color wheel

### 35.12 — White Space Doctrine

White space is a design element, not unused area. A sheet with insufficient white space communicates less, regardless of how much information it contains.

**Target:** 25–40% of a sheet remains open field in an editorial series.

### 35.13 — Sheet Anatomy

```
[Header zone]     Project name · Sheet title · Sheet number
[Content zone]    Dominant element + supporting elements
[Caption zone]    Explanatory text, aligned to the grid
[Footer zone]     Studio mark · Scale · Date · Stage label
```

Zones remain in identical positions across the entire series.

### 35.14 — Dominant Element Rule

Each sheet has exactly one dominant element occupying the largest visual weight. Two dominant elements on one sheet create competition and reduce comprehension.

### 35.15 — Supporting Element Rule

Supporting elements clarify the dominant element. An element that neither dominates nor supports must be removed.

### 35.16 — Information Density Control

| Sheet Role | Elements per Sheet |
|-----------|--------------------|
| Opening | 1 |
| Concept | 1–3 |
| Context | 2–4 |
| Organization | 3–6 |
| Experience | 1–3 |
| Detail | 3–6 |
| Closing | 1 |

Exceeding the range requires splitting the sheet, not shrinking the content.

### 35.17 — Caption Standard

Every image, drawing, and diagram carries a caption stating: what it shows, from where, and at what stage. An uncaptioned image transfers interpretation responsibility to the viewer.

### 35.18 — Sheet Numbering

```
[Series code]-[Chapter]-[Sheet]
Example: ED-03-02  →  Editorial series, Chapter 03, Sheet 02
```

### 35.19 — Cross-Reference Discipline

References between sheets and to system sections use plain, resolvable notation. Reference targets are written as section numbers and file names in plain text: `01_CORE.md` Section 25.13, `00_IDENTITY.md` Section 07, `02_LIBRARY.md` Section 03. Fabricated links, external URLs, or decorative reference marks are prohibited.

### 35.20 — Drawing Presentation Standard

| Element | Standard |
|---------|----------|
| Line weight | Follows Section 20.04 hierarchy |
| Poché | Solid fill for cut elements in presentation drawings |
| Context | Shown in a lighter tone, never at full weight |
| Scale bar | Present on every scaled drawing |
| North arrow | Present on every plan |
| Level marks | Present on every section |
| Annotation | Minimal on presentation drawings; full on documentation |

### 35.21 — Plan Presentation

Presentation plans show: spatial hierarchy, furniture where it clarifies use, floor material change, thresholds, and the relationship to outdoor space. They omit dimension strings and technical tags.

### 35.22 — Section Presentation

Presentation sections show: vertical relationship, light behavior, human figures, ground condition, and context beyond the cut. A section without ground and sky is incomplete.

### 35.23 — Elevation Presentation

Presentation elevations show: material differentiation, shadow depth, human scale, and adjacent context. A flat elevation without shadow misrepresents the façade.

### 35.24 — Diagram Standard

| Rule | Requirement |
|------|-------------|
| One idea | Each diagram explains exactly one concept |
| Abstraction | Only the information required by the idea is drawn |
| Consistency | The same visual convention across the whole series |
| Legend | Present when symbols are used |
| Sequence | Related diagrams read left to right or top to bottom |

### 35.25 — Diagram Types

```
Site and context      Massing and volume      Program and zoning
Circulation           Structure               Environmental strategy
Light and shadow      Material logic          Assembly and detail
Phasing               Experience sequence
```

### 35.26 — Diagram Color Logic

Diagram color communicates category, not decoration. The same category carries the same color across every diagram in the series.

### 35.27 — Image Placement Logic

| Placement | Use |
|-----------|-----|
| Full bleed | Opening, closing, and single-argument atmosphere sheets |
| Full column width | Primary supporting image |
| Half column | Comparative pairs |
| Inset | Detail reference within a larger drawing |

Images never bleed on only one edge without a compositional reason.

### 35.28 — Image Pairing Logic

Paired images must share: format, lighting logic, camera height, and level of realism. A pair that differs in these dimensions compares nothing.

### 35.29 — Image Cropping Discipline

Crop to strengthen the architectural argument. Never crop to hide unresolved design; unresolved design is reported, not concealed.

### 35.30 — Series Rhythm

An editorial series alternates density. A sequence of uniformly dense sheets exhausts the reader; a sequence of uniformly sparse sheets communicates insufficiently.

```
Low → Medium → High → Medium → Low → High → Low
```

### 35.31 — Opening Sheet Standard

The opening sheet presents one image and the project name. It establishes atmosphere and does not explain. Explanation begins on the second sheet.

### 35.32 — Closing Sheet Standard

The closing sheet resolves. It presents the completed architectural idea, not a summary of text. A series that ends on a technical sheet has no conclusion.

### 35.33 — Studio Mark Placement

The studio mark appears once per sheet, in the same position, at the same size, in the neutral structure color. It never competes with content.

### 35.34 — Stage Label Placement

Every sheet carries the stage label defined in Section 10.51 in the footer zone. This is a mandatory element, not a design option.

### 35.35 — Sheet Verification Checklist

| Check | Requirement |
|-------|-------------|
| Grid | All elements aligned |
| Hierarchy | One dominant element |
| Caption | Present and accurate |
| Typography | Within the defined scale and weights |
| Color | Within the project palette |
| White space | Within the target range |
| Stage label | Present |
| Numbering | Correct and continuous |
| Source fidelity | Verified against Section 10.21 |

### 35.36 — Image Generation Governance

All AI image production is governed by this subsection together with Sections 07.14, 10.21, 25.12, and 27.21. No visual generation occurs without a declared source state, a declared permission level, and a declared change scope.

### 35.37 — Pre-Generation Declaration

```
PRE-GENERATION DECLARATION
Purpose:            [What architectural argument the image serves]
Source state:       [Locked / Developing / Reference / None]
Permission level:   [Section 27.21 level]
Route:              [Section 25.12 route]
Locked items:       [Immutable geometry register]
Permitted change:   [Explicit list]
Stage label:        [Concept / DD / Preliminary / Final]
```

**No prompt is written before this declaration exists.**

### 35.38 — Prompt Architecture

Every architectural prompt is constructed in a fixed order:

```
01 Subject and building type
02 Geometry constraints (from the locked register)
03 Camera: position, height, lens, angle
04 Light: time, season, direction, quality
05 Materials: named, with finish and scale
06 Context: site, neighbors, vegetation, ground
07 Atmosphere: weather, mood, human activity
08 Technical quality: resolution, realism level, rendering character
09 Prohibitions: the negative block (Section 10.48)
```

### 35.39 — Prompt Language Rule

All prompts are written in English regardless of the conversation language. Prompt vocabulary is architectural and specific: material names, finish descriptions, lens values, and light conditions — never subjective adjectives alone.

### 35.40 — Prompt Specificity Standard

| Weak | Strong |
|------|--------|
| "modern building" | "four-storey residential building, horizontal concrete bands, full-height glazing" |
| "nice lighting" | "late afternoon sun, low western angle, long soft shadows, warm 4200K" |
| "stone facade" | "honed travertine cladding, 600×300 mm panels, 8 mm open joints" |
| "beautiful render" | "architectural photography, 35 mm lens, two-point perspective, verticals corrected" |

### 35.41 — Negative Prompt Standard

Every architectural prompt includes prohibitions covering: geometry change, floor count change, opening change, added elements, distorted scale, impossible structure, text artifacts, watermark, oversaturation, and fisheye distortion.

### 35.42 — Camera Prompt Standard

```
Camera height:  1.60 m (human eye level) unless specified
Lens:           24–35 mm context · 35–50 mm natural · 85 mm+ detail
Perspective:    Two-point, verticals corrected
Distance:       Sufficient for the full subject plus context
Framing:        Subject dominant, horizon controlled
```

### 35.43 — Light Prompt Standard

| Condition | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| Morning | Low eastern sun, cool-neutral, long shadows, clear atmosphere |
| Midday | High sun, short shadows, high contrast — avoided for exteriors |
| Late afternoon | Low western sun, warm, long soft shadows — default for exteriors |
| Blue hour | Even ambient, interior light dominant — default for night identity |
| Overcast | Soft even light, material texture readable — default for material studies |

### 35.44 — Material Prompt Standard

Every material is named with: material, finish, format or module, joint condition, and color tone. A material without a stated scale will be rendered at an arbitrary and usually wrong scale.

### 35.45 — Context Prompt Standard

Context is specified as: ground surface, adjacent building height and character, vegetation species type, street condition, and sky condition. Unspecified context is invented by the model and constitutes an unauthorized claim.

### 35.46 — Editorial Publication Signature

This is the studio's signature visual output format, referenced by `00_IDENTITY.md` Section 07.05.

**Definition:** A sequenced set of sheets that presents a project as an architectural publication — with chapters, narrative progression, controlled density, and a consistent graphic system.

| Attribute | Standard |
|-----------|----------|
| Structure | Chapters following Section 17.02 |
| Density rhythm | Section 35.30 |
| Grid | One grid across the entire series (Section 35.04) |
| Typography | One system across the entire series (Section 35.06) |
| Color | Derived from the project material palette (Section 35.10) |
| Image logic | One lighting logic, one realism level (Section 25.11) |
| Caption discipline | Every visual captioned (Section 35.17) |
| Opening and closing | Sections 35.31 and 35.32 |
| Verification | Section 35.35 per sheet, Section 10.52 for the series |

**Signature characteristics:** generous white space, quiet typography, material-derived color, drawings treated as images, and an argument that builds from context to resolution.

### 35.47 — Editorial Chapter Definition

Each chapter declares: its question, its dominant medium, its sheet count, and its contribution to the argument. A chapter without a question is a folder, not a chapter.

### 35.48 — Editorial Sequence Construction

```
Establish the place       →  Context chapter
State the question        →  Concept chapter
Present the response      →  Strategy chapter
Prove the organization    →  Plan and section chapter
Communicate the experience →  Interior and human-scale chapter
Demonstrate the resolution →  Material and detail chapter
Close the argument        →  Resolution chapter
```

### 35.49 — Editorial Text Standard

Editorial text is short, architectural, and evidential. Each chapter carries one paragraph maximum of body text; the drawings and images carry the argument.

### 35.50 — Editorial Direction Brief

Before production of an editorial series, the Section 09.16 cell produces:

```
EDITORIAL_DIRECTION_BRIEF
Source status register:  [What exists, what state, what is missing]
Narrative sequence:      [Chapter list with questions]
Sheet personalities:     [Role and density per sheet]
Required assets:         [Images, drawings, diagrams to produce]
Unresolved assumptions:  [Declared]
Production mode:         [Manual / AI-assisted / Hybrid]
Approval checkpoint:     [Where Majid approves]
```

### 35.51 — Early Client Concept Visual Standard

An early client image communicates one idea. It is deliberately less resolved than a final visualization and is labelled `Concept`.

| Attribute | Standard |
|-----------|----------|
| Realism | Controlled — atmospheric rather than photographic |
| Detail | Sufficient to communicate the idea, no more |
| Material | Indicative, declared as indicative |
| Context | Simplified but plausible |
| People | Present, for scale and life |
| Label | `Concept — not final design` |

### 35.52 — Early Visual Direction Card

Produced by the Section 09.17 cell:

```
EARLY_VISUAL_DIRECTION_CARD
Image type:            [Exterior / Interior / Aerial / Atmosphere]
Meeting purpose:       [Decision required from the client]
Design option status:  [Single option / Comparative]
Source constraints:    [Confirmed items]
Permitted variation:   [Explicit list]
Camera and light:      [Direction]
Title:                 [Sheet title]
Concept sentence:      [Optional Persian sentence for the client]
Client risk note:      [What could be misread]
```

### 35.53 — Comparative Option Presentation

When two or more options are presented, they must be shown from the identical camera, in identical light, at identical realism. Any difference other than the design itself invalidates the comparison.

### 35.54 — Progressive Resolution Rule

Visual resolution increases with project phase. Presenting a photographic image at concept stage creates commitment before the design is resolved.

```
Concept        →  Atmospheric, indicative
Schematic      →  Clear geometry, indicative material
Design Dev     →  Accurate geometry, specified material
Documentation  →  Technical, precise
Final          →  Photographic, verified
```

### 35.55 — Exterior Visualization Standard

| Element | Standard |
|---------|----------|
| Camera | Eye level, two-point, verticals corrected |
| Sun | Low angle, direction consistent with site orientation |
| Shadow | Present, directional, consistent with the sun position |
| Sky | Real gradient, not a flat color |
| Ground | Material-specific, wet or dry declared |
| Vegetation | Climate-appropriate species |
| Neighbors | Present when they affect perception |
| People | Correctly scaled, purposefully placed |
| Vehicles | Contemporary, correctly scaled, non-dominant |

### 35.56 — Interior Visualization Standard

| Element | Standard |
|---------|----------|
| Camera | 1.50–1.60 m, 24–35 mm, verticals corrected |
| Daylight | Primary light source, direction visible |
| Artificial light | Layered per Section 24.05 |
| Materials | Correct texture scale and reflectivity |
| Furniture | Correctly scaled, consistent with the design intent |
| Ceiling | Visible, resolved, not cropped away to avoid detail |
| View out | Consistent with the site context |

### 35.57 — Aerial and Context Visualization

Aerial views show the project's urban relationship. The surrounding fabric must be represented honestly, including elements that are unfavorable to the project.

### 35.58 — Night Visualization Standard

Night images communicate the building's light identity: which spaces glow, how the façade reads, how the entrance is found, and how the building contributes to the street at night.

### 35.59 — Detail Visualization Standard

Detail images prove material quality: junction resolution, texture at close range, shadow depth, and the honesty of the assembly.

### 35.60 — Human Presence Standard

People in images are: correctly scaled, contextually appropriate in dress and activity, non-distracting, and never used decoratively in a way that misrepresents occupancy.

### 35.61 — Atmosphere Control

Atmosphere is created by light, material, and composition — not by post-production filters, lens flares, or artificial haze applied uniformly.

### 35.62 — Post-Production Standard for Sheets

Permitted: exposure, contrast, white balance, local dodging and burning, lens correction, and controlled sharpening.

Prohibited: geometric alteration, element insertion or removal, material replacement, and sky replacement that contradicts the declared light condition.

### 35.63 — Output Resolution Standard

| Medium | Resolution |
|--------|------------|
| A3 print sheet | 300 dpi at final size |
| A1 print sheet | 200–300 dpi at final size |
| Screen presentation | 1920 px minimum on the long edge |
| Social square | 1080 × 1080 px minimum |
| Social vertical | 1080 × 1920 px |
| Archive master | Maximum available, uncompressed |

### 35.64 — File Format Standard

| Purpose | Format |
|---------|--------|
| Print delivery | PDF, embedded fonts, CMYK where required |
| Screen delivery | PDF or PNG |
| Image master | TIFF or PNG, 16-bit where available |
| Working image | PSD with layers retained |
| Social output | JPG, high quality |

### 35.65 — Visual Delivery Record

Every visual delivery records: asset list, versions, stage labels, source register references, and approval. Section 28.16 governs the register.

### 35.66 — Social Media Visual Standard

Social output is a compressed argument. One idea, immediately readable, with the studio's graphic discipline intact.

| Format | Use |
|--------|-----|
| Square | Single image, project announcement |
| Vertical story | Sequence, process, detail focus |
| Carousel | Chapter-based argument, 5–8 frames |

### 35.67 — Social Typography

Social typography follows the studio system at increased scale. Minimum readable size on a phone governs; the print scale does not transfer directly.

### 35.68 — Social Caption Standard

Social captions state: project, location, stage, and the one architectural idea. Marketing language and generic praise are prohibited.

### 35.69 — Social Sequence Logic

```
Frame 01  Atmosphere — one strong image
Frame 02  Context — where and why
Frame 03  Idea — the concept in one diagram
Frame 04  Organization — plan or section
Frame 05  Experience — interior or human scale
Frame 06  Material — detail
Frame 07  Resolution — the closing image
```

### 35.70 — Confidentiality in Social Output

No client name, address, fee, or unapproved image is published. Approval for publication is recorded before production, not after.

### 35.71 — Portfolio Visual Standard

The portfolio uses the editorial system at reduced length. Each project occupies a fixed number of sheets with an identical internal structure, so that projects are comparable and the studio's thinking is visible.

```
Sheet 01  Atmosphere and project identity
Sheet 02  Context and question
Sheet 03  Idea and strategy
Sheet 04  Organization — plan and section
Sheet 05  Experience and material
Sheet 06  Resolution
```

### 35.72 — Competition Board Standard

Competition boards are read at distance first and at detail second.

| Reading Distance | Must Communicate |
|------------------|------------------|
| 3 m | The idea, through one dominant image or diagram |
| 1 m | The organization, through plans and sections |
| 0.3 m | The resolution, through detail and text |

**Rule:** A board that requires close reading to reveal its idea has failed at the first reading distance.

### 35.73 — Award and Publication Submission Standard

Submissions follow the organizer's format exactly. Within that format, the studio's graphic discipline is maintained. Format compliance is verified before design begins, not after.

### 35.74 — Studio Brand Asset System

| Asset | Definition |
|-------|------------|
| Studio mark | The primary identifier, one form, one proportion |
| Mark variants | Full, compact, and single-color versions only |
| Typeface set | The primary and secondary families defined in Section 35.06 |
| Color set | The neutral system defined in Section 35.10 |
| Sheet templates | Per format, per output type |
| Document templates | Proposal, report, specification, transmittal |

### 35.75 — Studio Mark Usage Rules

- One mark per sheet or document page
- Fixed clear space equal to the mark's height on all sides
- Never stretched, rotated, outlined, or shadowed
- Never placed over a busy image area
- Never recolored outside the defined color set

### 35.76 — Document Template System

Every studio document uses a template with: fixed margins, fixed heading hierarchy, fixed table style, fixed footer with document identity, and a consistent page numbering system.

### 35.77 — Proposal and Report Graphic Standard

Proposals and reports are typographic documents, not brochures. Images support the argument; they do not fill space. Section 14.05 defines the content structure; this subsection governs its appearance.

### 35.78 — Drawing Sheet Template Standard

| Element | Position |
|---------|----------|
| Title block | Right edge or bottom edge, consistent across the set |
| Project identity | Top of the title block |
| Sheet title and number | Bottom of the title block, largest elements within it |
| Revision table | Above or beside the title block |
| Scale and north | Adjacent to the drawing, not only in the title block |
| Notes | Fixed column position |

### 35.79 — Visual Archive Structure

```
06_VISUALIZATION/
├── 01_SOURCE/          Renders, photographs, model exports
├── 02_WORKING/         Layered working files
├── 03_GENERATED/       AI outputs with generation records
├── 04_APPROVED/        Verified, labelled, delivery-ready
├── 05_SHEETS/          Composed sheets and series
└── 06_DELIVERED/       Issued packages with delivery records
```

### 35.80 — Visual Naming Convention

```
[ProjectCode]_[Type]_[View]_[Stage]_[Version]_[Date]
Example Reference Only: MA24_EXT_SouthEntry_CON_V04_20260811 — `MA24` is an illustrative project code, not a declared studio convention.
```

Type codes: `EXT` exterior · `INT` interior · `AER` aerial · `DET` detail · `DIA` diagram · `PLN` plan · `SEC` section · `ELE` elevation · `SHT` sheet.

### 35.81 — AI Artifact Catalogue

| Artifact | Detection | Correction |
|----------|-----------|------------|
| Warped verticals | Compare with source geometry | Regenerate with perspective constraint or correct in post |
| Duplicated elements | Count openings, columns, floors against source | Regenerate with an explicit count constraint |
| Impossible structure | Trace load paths visually | Regenerate with a structural constraint statement |
| Melted material texture | Inspect at 100% zoom | Regenerate at higher resolution or upscale with detail control |
| Invented text or signage | Scan all surfaces | Add a text prohibition and mask-correct |
| Scale-inconsistent people | Compare against door and step heights | Mask and replace |
| Impossible vegetation | Check species against climate | Regenerate with a species constraint |
| Inconsistent shadows | Trace shadow directions to one sun position | Regenerate with an explicit sun-angle statement |
| Over-saturated atmosphere | Compare with the declared light condition | Correct in post-production |
| Blurred or invented context | Compare with site data | Mask, replace, or declare as indicative |

### 35.82 — Artifact Correction Protocol

```
Detect → Classify → Determine whether the cause is prompt, route, or source →
Correct the cause, not only the symptom → Regenerate or mask-correct →
Re-verify against the source → Record the artifact type in the project register
```

### 35.83 — Upscaling Standard

Upscaling increases resolution and material detail. It must not alter geometry, add elements, or change material identity. Every upscaled output is compared with its input before acceptance.

### 35.84 — Masking and Inpainting Standard

```
01 Define the change area precisely
02 Create the mask with a controlled edge
03 State what the masked area must become
04 State that everything outside the mask is unchanged
05 Generate
06 Verify the unmasked area is pixel-consistent with the source
07 Blend only within the mask boundary
```

**Any change detected outside the mask is a Critical error under Section 10.06.**

### 35.85 — Iteration Record

```
ITERATION RECORD
Iteration:        [Number]
Route:            [Section 25.12 route]
Changed constraint: [What was modified from the previous attempt]
Result:           [Accepted / Rejected]
Reason:           [Why]
```

Iteration without a changed constraint is prohibited under Section 10.50.

### 35.86 — Visual Gate 05 Verification

Before a visual output passes Gate 05:

| Check | Reference |
|-------|-----------|
| Source fidelity | Section 10.21 |
| Geometry lock respected | Section 10.22 |
| Design drift absent | Section 10.23 |
| Artifacts absent | Section 35.81 |
| Scale plausible | Section 10.34 |
| Material consistent | Section 10.35 |
| Lighting consistent | Section 10.36 |
| Stage labelled | Section 10.51 |
| Register entry complete | Section 28.16 |
| Sheet standard met | Section 35.35 |

### 35.87 — Visual Failure Modes

| Failure | Consequence |
|---------|-------------|
| Photographic realism at concept stage | False client commitment |
| Unlabelled AI enhancement | Professional credibility risk |
| Inconsistent series lighting | The set reads as unrelated projects |
| Decorative graphic effects | Perceived as compensation for weak design |
| Hidden unresolved areas | Discovered later at higher cost |
| Invented context | Unsupportable claim about the site |
| Over-dense sheets | The argument is not read |

### 35.88 — Visual Consistency Across Media

The same project must read identically in print, on screen, and on social media. Color management, crop logic, and typography scale are adapted; identity and hierarchy are not.

### 35.89 — Visual Communication Accessibility

Contrast must remain sufficient for readability. Information must never be carried by color alone; a legend, label, or pattern accompanies every color-coded system.

### 35.90 — Print Production Standard

Verify before printing: bleed, color profile, image resolution at final size, font embedding, line weights at scale, and a printed proof of one representative sheet.

### 35.91 — Screen Presentation Standard

Screen presentation uses the same grid at screen aspect ratio. Text size is increased for viewing distance. Animation between sheets is minimal and never decorative.

### 35.92 — Physical Model Photography Standard

Models are photographed on a neutral field, with controlled directional light, at eye level relative to the model's scale, with the depth of field managed so the architecture reads clearly.

### 35.93 — Video and Animation Standard

| Element | Standard |
|---------|----------|
| Camera movement | Slow, purposeful, architectural |
| Duration | Determined by the argument, not by available footage |
| Cut logic | Each cut advances the spatial narrative |
| Sound | Optional, never dominant |
| Text | Minimal, in the studio typographic system |
| Ending | Resolves on a held image |

### 35.94 — Visual Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Locked source | Approved design that must not be altered |
| Geometry register | The recorded list of immutable elements |
| Design drift | Unauthorized change introduced during a visual operation |
| Dominant element | The single largest visual weight on a sheet |
| Density rhythm | The planned variation of information across a series |
| Stage label | The declaration of the design phase an image represents |
| Editorial series | The studio's signature sequenced sheet format |
| Negative block | The prohibition list within a prompt |

### 35.95 — Visual Trend Observation Protocol

Visual trends are observed systematically and recorded in `02_LIBRARY.md` Section 03. Each observation records: what is changing, where it appears, why it is spreading, and what architectural need it addresses.

```
TREND OBSERVATION
Trend:            [What]
Domain:           [Rendering / Graphic / Presentation / Social / Tool]
First observed:   [Date and source]
Frequency:        [Isolated / Emerging / Established]
Underlying need:  [What problem it solves]
Studio relevance: [High / Medium / Low / None]
```

### 35.96 — Benchmark Analysis Method

Benchmarking studies how a reference achieves its result, not how it looks.

```
01 Identify the reference and its context
02 Describe the effect it achieves
03 Analyze the mechanism: grid, hierarchy, light, material, restraint
04 Extract the transferable principle
05 Test the principle against the studio's identity
06 Record the principle, never the imagery
```

### 35.97 — Trend Adoption Filter

| Filter | Question |
|--------|----------|
| Identity | Does it strengthen or dilute the studio's visual character? |
| Longevity | Will it read as dated within two years? |
| Substance | Does it communicate information or only style? |
| Feasibility | Can it be produced consistently across a series? |
| Client value | Does it improve client understanding? |

**A trend passing fewer than four filters is recorded as observation only and not adopted.**

### 35.98 — Visual Language Evolution Record

Every approved change to the studio's visual language records: what changed, why, which projects it affects, what it replaces, and the date. Visual identity evolves deliberately, never by accumulation.

### 35.99 — Visual Identity Protection Rule

The studio's visual identity is not adjusted per project or per client preference. A client may influence the content and emphasis of a presentation. A client does not redefine the studio's graphic language.

**Exception:** When a client's own brand system governs the deliverable, the studio applies the client's system explicitly and records the deviation. The studio's system remains the default.

### 35.100 — Visual Identity Principle

```
One grid. One type system. One palette from the project.
One idea per sheet. One argument per series.
Lock the truth. Label the stage. Verify before delivery.
Evolve deliberately. Never decorate to compensate.
```

## 36 — Iranian Regulatory Intelligence Engine

> Defines the structured handling of Iranian building regulation, municipal process, and local compliance verification.

### 36.01 — Purpose and Boundary

This section structures how the system reasons about Iranian regulation. It does not certify compliance. Official verification by the responsible licensed engineer and the relevant authority is always required.

### 36.02 — Regulatory Framework Map

| Framework | Domain |
|-----------|--------|
| National Building Regulations (22 topics) | Technical requirements across all disciplines |
| Municipality regulations | Zoning, density, height, setback, occupancy, projection, parking |
| Comprehensive and detailed urban plans | Land use, density, permitted uses |
| Fire department requirements | Escape, access, firefighting provision |
| Engineering Organization requirements | Design responsibility, supervision, submission |
| Local ordinances | City-specific variations |

### 36.03 — National Building Regulations Topic Reference

```
Topic 01  Definitions                    Topic 12  Safety during construction
Topic 02  Administrative                 Topic 13  Electrical installations
Topic 03  Fire protection                Topic 14  Mechanical installations
Topic 04  General building requirements  Topic 15  Lifts and escalators
Topic 05  Building materials             Topic 16  Plumbing and sanitary
Topic 06  Loads on buildings             Topic 17  Gas installations
Topic 07  Foundations                    Topic 18  Sound insulation
Topic 08  Masonry buildings              Topic 19  Energy conservation
Topic 09  Reinforced concrete            Topic 20  Signage and safety
Topic 10  Steel structures               Topic 21  Passive defence
Topic 11  Industrialized systems         Topic 22  Maintenance and operation
```

**Rule:** Topic references orient the analysis. The current official text governs and must be consulted for any binding statement.

### 36.04 — Municipal Parameter Register

Before design begins, the following must be obtained and recorded, never assumed:

```
MUNICIPAL PARAMETER REGISTER
Land use:                [Permitted uses]
Plot area:               [m², per official document]
Density (occupancy):     [% of plot]
Floor area ratio:        [Permitted]
Permitted floors:        [Count]
Maximum height:          [m]
Setbacks:                [Front / rear / side]
Projection allowance:    [Depth and conditions]
Parking requirement:     [Spaces per unit or area]
Green space requirement: [% or area]
Access restrictions:     [Street width, corner conditions]
Source:                  [Document and date]
Verification status:     [Verified / Requires verification]
```

### 36.05 — Verification Discipline

Every regulatory statement carries a status:

| Status | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| Verified | Official text or official document available and cited |
| Indicative | Common practice; requires confirmation |
| Requires Verification | Not confirmed; must not be relied upon |

**The system never states compliance. It states the verification status.**

### 36.06 — Common Compliance Risk Areas

| Area | Typical Risk |
|------|--------------|
| Projection over the setback | Depth and height conditions misapplied |
| Parking count and ramp geometry | Insufficient spaces or non-compliant ramp slope |
| Escape distance and stair width | Exceeded travel distance, insufficient width |
| Light and ventilation courts | Undersized shafts for the served rooms |
| Height measurement datum | Measured from the wrong reference level |
| Basement extent and access | Excavation limits and ventilation |
| Facade projection over the street | Municipal envelope violation |
| Accessibility provision | Missing accessible route or facility |
| Energy compliance (Topic 19) | Envelope performance not demonstrated |
| Passive defence (Topic 21) | Requirements omitted from early planning |

### 36.07 — Regulation Impact on Design Decisions

Regulatory constraints are introduced at concept stage, not at permit stage. A concept developed outside the regulatory envelope generates rework, cost, and client distrust.

### 36.08 — Regulatory Conflict Handling

When a design intent conflicts with a regulation:

1. State the regulation and its verification status
2. State the design intent
3. Identify whether an exception, variance, or alternative interpretation exists
4. Present compliant alternatives
5. Recommend the option that best preserves the design intent
6. Record the decision and required official confirmation

### 36.09 — Permit Process Awareness

```
Site document verification → Municipal parameter confirmation →
Preliminary design → Engineering Organization submission →
Structural and MEP design → Permit issue →
Construction supervision → Completion certificate
```

Each stage has documentation requirements that affect the design programme and must be planned, not discovered.

### 36.10 — Responsibility Boundary

| Responsibility | Holder |
|----------------|--------|
| Design compliance intent | Architect |
| Structural verification | Structural engineer |
| MEP verification | MEP engineer |
| Regulatory approval | Municipality and Engineering Organization |
| Site compliance | Supervising engineer |
| System role | Structured analysis and risk identification only |

### 36.11 — Regulatory Knowledge Recording

Regulatory findings are recorded in `02_LIBRARY.md` with: the requirement, the source document, the date, the city, and the verification status. Regulation changes; every entry must be dated and city-specific.

### 36.12 — Regulatory Principle

```
Obtain the parameters. Design within the envelope.
State the verification status. Never certify.
```

## 37 — Architectural Business Intelligence Engine

> Defines structured analysis of project viability, studio capacity, and long-term practice development.

### 37.01 — Purpose

Sections 14 and 30 define business structure and judgment. Section 37 defines the analytical engine that supports strategic decisions about which work to take and how the practice develops.

### 37.02 — Project Viability Analysis

```
PROJECT VIABILITY ANALYSIS
Identity fit:          [High / Medium / Low]
Technical capability:  [Within capacity / Requires support / Beyond capacity]
Client maturity:       [Decisive / Uncertain / Unstable]
Budget realism:        [Realistic / Tight / Unrealistic]
Schedule feasibility:  [Feasible / Compressed / Impossible]
Regulatory complexity: [Low / Medium / High]
Portfolio value:       [High / Medium / Low]
Learning value:        [High / Medium / Low]
Risk summary:          [Principal risks]
Recommendation:        [Pursue / Pursue with conditions / Decline]
```

### 37.03 — Effort Estimation Logic

```
Base effort by building type and area
    × Complexity factor (geometry, systems, regulation)
    × Client factor (decision speed, revision behavior)
    × Schedule factor (compression premium)
    + Visualization and presentation effort
    + Coordination effort
    + Contingency
```

Estimated effort is recorded and compared with actual effort at project close, improving future estimation accuracy.

### 37.04 — Capacity Management

| Indicator | Warning Condition |
|-----------|-------------------|
| Concurrent active projects | Exceeds the number that can be reviewed properly |
| Overlapping deadline peaks | Two or more milestones in the same week |
| Unresolved decision backlog | Client decisions pending across multiple projects |
| Rework proportion | Rising above the historical baseline |

**Accepting work beyond capacity damages quality on existing projects. Capacity is a design decision.**

### 37.05 — Fee Benchmarking Record

Each project records: building type, area, service scope, fee, effort, and outcome. The accumulated record creates the studio's own benchmark, which is more reliable than market generalization.

### 37.06 — Client Portfolio Balance

| Client Type | Strategic Role |
|-------------|----------------|
| Repeat clients | Stability and predictable revenue |
| Referral clients | Growth with reduced acquisition effort |
| Portfolio projects | Identity development and visibility |
| Learning projects | Capability expansion |

A portfolio composed entirely of one type is strategically fragile.

### 37.07 — Practice Development Metrics

| Metric | Direction |
|--------|-----------|
| Average project quality (AQS) | Increasing |
| Rework proportion | Decreasing |
| Estimation accuracy | Improving |
| Repeat and referral share | Increasing |
| Typology range | Deliberate, not accidental |
| Published or recognized work | Growing |

### 37.08 — Strategic Positioning

The studio's position is defined by what it does exceptionally, not by what it can do adequately. Positioning statements derive from `00_IDENTITY.md`, not from market opportunity.

### 37.09 — Decline Discipline

Declining work is a professional decision recorded with its reason. A recorded decline informs future positioning and prevents repeated evaluation of unsuitable opportunities.

### 37.10 — Business Intelligence Recording

Viability analyses, effort comparisons, fee outcomes, and decline decisions are recorded in `02_LIBRARY.md` as business knowledge, subject to the admission criteria in Section 11.03.

### 37.11 — Business Intelligence Principle

```
Analyze before accepting. Estimate from record, not from hope.
Protect capacity. Position by strength.
```

## 38 — Client Communication Intelligence

> Defines structured client interaction, decision facilitation, and expectation control.

### 38.01 — Purpose

Design quality is delivered through communication. This section defines how information reaches the client so that decisions are informed, timely, and stable.

### 38.02 — Communication Objectives

| Objective | Definition |
|-----------|------------|
| Clarity | The client understands what is being decided |
| Confidence | The client trusts the reasoning |
| Timeliness | Decisions arrive when the programme requires them |
| Stability | Decisions remain made |
| Boundary | The client understands scope, stage, and limitation |

### 38.03 — Client Language Discipline

Client communication uses the client's language and the client's frame of reference. Architectural terminology is translated into experience, cost, time, and consequence.

| Instead of | Say |
|------------|-----|
| "The massing is stepped" | "The upper floors are set back, creating terraces and more daylight below" |
| "We are optimizing the net-to-gross ratio" | "We are increasing usable area without increasing construction cost" |
| "The envelope requires a thermal break" | "This detail prevents heat loss and condensation at the junction" |

### 38.04 — Decision Framing

Every decision presented to a client includes: the decision required, the options, the consequence of each option, the recommendation, the reason, and the deadline.

```
CLIENT DECISION FRAME
Decision:          [What must be decided]
Options:           [A / B / C with brief description]
Consequences:      [Cost / time / quality / experience per option]
Recommendation:    [Which and why]
Deadline:          [When the decision is required]
Cost of delay:     [Programme or cost impact]
```

### 38.05 — Option Discipline

Present two or three developed options, never many undeveloped ones. Choice without evaluation transfers the architect's responsibility to the client.

### 38.06 — Expectation Setting

At every stage the client is told: what this stage produces, what it does not produce, what remains uncertain, and what the next stage resolves.

### 38.07 — Meeting Structure

```
01 Purpose and required decisions
02 Progress since the last meeting
03 Presentation of the material
04 Discussion and questions
05 Decisions recorded
06 Actions with owners and dates
07 Next meeting purpose
```

### 38.08 — Meeting Record Discipline

Every meeting produces a written record of decisions and actions, issued within a defined period. A verbal decision is confirmed in writing before it is acted upon.

### 38.09 — Change Request Handling

```
Received → Classified (included / minor / scope change) →
Impact stated (design / cost / time) → Decision requested →
Recorded → Implemented
```

**No change is implemented before it is classified and recorded.**

### 38.10 — Difficult Conversation Protocol

When delivering unwelcome information — cost increase, regulatory obstacle, schedule impact, or design limitation:

1. State the issue directly and early
2. State the cause factually, without blame
3. State the consequence
4. Present the options
5. Recommend
6. Define the decision required and by when

**Delaying unwelcome information converts a manageable problem into a relationship failure.**

### 38.11 — Client Education

Where a client lacks the vocabulary to evaluate a decision, the studio supplies it: a reference, a comparison, a diagram, or a sample. An educated client makes faster and more stable decisions.

### 38.12 — Feedback Interpretation

Client feedback is interpreted, not implemented literally. A client statement describes a symptom; the architect identifies the cause.

| Client Says | Possible Meaning |
|-------------|------------------|
| "It feels cold" | Material palette, light quality, or proportion |
| "It looks expensive" | Perceived complexity or unfamiliar material |
| "It's too modern" | Unfamiliar form language or absence of familiar reference |
| "Can we make it bigger?" | Perceived insufficiency of a specific space, not the whole |
| "I don't like it" | Unstated priority not addressed in the brief |

**Ask which part and why before changing anything.**

### 38.13 — Silence Interpretation

Client silence is not approval. Approval is explicit, recorded, and dated.

### 38.14 — Communication Frequency

Communication is regular and predictable. An unexpected silence from the studio is interpreted by the client as inactivity, regardless of the work being done.

### 38.15 — Handover Communication

At delivery the client receives: what was produced, how to use it, what it does not cover, who is responsible for what, and what the next steps are.

### 38.16 — Relationship Record

Each client relationship records: communication preferences, decision behavior, priorities, sensitivities, and outcomes. This record improves future collaboration and informs Section 30.02.

### 38.17 — Client Communication Principle

```
Translate the architecture. Frame the decision. Record the answer.
Deliver bad news early. Never mistake silence for agreement.
```
